qs.q: An echocardiogram of a newborn reveals a large defect in the lower part of the interatrial septum, accompanied by a cleft mitral valve. Which embryological structure failed to develop properly?
o: Fused anterior and posterior endocardial cushions
Fenestrated superior region of the septum primum
Muscular extension of the secondary atrial fold
Aortopulmonary spiral septum in outflow tract
Right horn incorporation into sinus venosus
qs.e: Endocardial cushion fusion divides the AV canal and forms the lower part of the atrial septum (ostium primum).
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Embryology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A newborn infant presents with a cleft lip and palate. During reconstructive planning, the surgical team notes that primary lip repair is typically performed at around 3 months of age, following the physiological 'rule of tens'. Which parameter is part of this famous clinical rule?
qs.e: The rule of tens for cleft lip repair includes 10 weeks of age, 10 pounds of weight, and a hemoglobin level of 10 grams per deciliter.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Surgery Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 60-year-old man is recovering in the surgical ICU following an oesophagectomy. As part of the prevention bundle for ventilator-associated pneumonia, at what angle should the head of his bed be strictly maintained?
qs.e: The ICU bundle for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia mandates elevating the head of the bed between 30 and 45 degrees to reduce the risk of micro-aspiration of gastric contents. Flat positioning significantly increases VAP incidence.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 45‑year‑old man with a 3‑month history of epigastric pain that wakes him at night and is relieved by eating food undergoes upper GI endoscopy, which shows an ulcer in the first part of the duodenum. What is the most likely pathophysiologic mechanism responsible for this ulcer?
o: Autoimmune parietal cell destruction leading to low acid
Gastrinoma causing extreme hypersecretion of gastric acid
Antral gastritis with increased gastrin and acid output
qs.e: Antral gastritis raises gastrin and acid, producing duodenal ulcers; body gastritis reduces acid and is more associated with gastric ulcers.
qs.s: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Its Surgical Complications: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends her annual clinical review. As part of comprehensive preventative care to reduce the incidence of diabetic foot complications, which intervention should be performed annually for every diabetic patient?
qs.e: Annual foot screening for every diabetic is a core component of prevention alongside risk stratification and education. Bone biopsy and casting are therapeutic interventions rather than routine annual screening tools.
qs.s: Diabetic Foot Ulcers: Neuropathy, Infection and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour undergoes retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) as part of his staging and treatment. He later complains of dry ejaculations during orgasm. What is the most likely cause of this complication?
o: Destruction of seminal vesicles by chemotherapy.
Permanent blockage of the penile urethra.
Retrograde ejaculation due to nerve damage.
qs.e: Retrograde ejaculation is a well-known complication of RPLND caused by nerve damage, though nerve-sparing techniques help mitigate this risk. Cisplatin causes ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neuropathy.
qs.s: Testicular Tumours, Hydrocele and Varicocele: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old man undergoes an abdominal ultrasound as part of an evaluation for lower urinary tract symptoms. Which measurement obtained during this scan is generally considered the upper limit of normal for post-void residual urine?
qs.e: A normal post-void residual urine volume on abdominal ultrasound is under 30 mL. Higher volumes indicate inefficient bladder emptying secondary to outlet obstruction or detrusor failure.
qs.s: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and Acute Urinary Retention: MCQs

qs.q: A premature infant with Bell stage IIA necrotising enterocolitis is placed on nil by mouth. For how long is enteral feeding typically withheld as part of the primary bowel rest management?
qs.e: Management of stages I and II includes stopping all enteral feeds for 7 to 14 days to achieve bowel rest. Gastric decompression with an orogastric or nasogastric tube is also maintained.
qs.s: Necrotising Enterocolitis in the Newborn: MCQs

es.q: List and explain the hand hygiene steps required as part of aseptic technique.
es.m:
**Hand hygiene requirements:**
- Wash hands thoroughly before handling any cultures or samples.
- Wash hands thoroughly after handling cultures or samples.
- Use proper washing technique to remove potential contaminants from the skin.
- Perform hand hygiene each time the hands may become contaminated during laboratory work.
es.s: Aseptic Techniques in Microbiology Laboratory: Essay questions

es.q: As part of a forensic investigation involving a suspected poisoning, the role of the liver in metabolism and excretion is crucial. Outline the primary functions of bile in the human body.
es.m: Bile plays two primary functions essential for bodily health: 1. **Elimination:** It facilitates the excretion of water-insoluble substances, including bilirubin, excess cholesterol, and various xenobiotics (foreign compounds) from the body. 2. **Emulsification:** In the gut, bile emulsifies dietary fats, a critical step for their digestion and absorption.

ai.title: Lower Uterine Segment Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The lower uterine segment is the thin, contractile part of the uterus that expands during labour. Understanding its location, relations and blood supply is essential for managing obstetric emergencies in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The lower uterine segment (LUS) forms the inferior third of the uterus during the third trimester and is the site of the uterine incision in most caesarean sections.
b: Thin muscular wall, expands with fetal descent
Visible on ultrasound as a hypoechoic line above the bladder

sections.p: The LUS lies between the uterine body above and the cervix below, extending from the internal os to the bladder reflection.
b: Anteriorly attached to the bladder peritoneum
Posteriorly related to the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas)

sections.p: Its close relationship to the bladder and rectum makes surgical dissection hazardous.
b: Bladder dome lies directly anterior
Rectum lies posterior, especially in a retroverted uterus

sections.p: Arterial supply derives mainly from the uterine arteries, with contributions from the ovarian arteries.
b: Uterine artery branches penetrate the myometrium
Anastomoses with ovarian arteries at the lateral uterine border

sections.p: Parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves and sympathetic fibers from the hypogastric plexus innervate the LUS, mediating uterine contractility.
b: Pain from LUS incision transmitted via T10‑L1 dermatomes

sections.p: During labour the LUS stretches, allowing the fetus to descend while maintaining uterine contractile force.
b: Provides a site for safe caesarean incision
Reduces risk of uterine rupture compared with upper segment

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, LUS injuries are common during emergency caesarean sections and obstetric hysterectomy.
b: Uterine rupture at the LUS can cause massive haemorrhage
Bladder injury occurs if incision is placed too low

t.b: Is the LUS thinned or ruptured? – A thin, hypoechoic line suggests a normal LUS; loss of continuity indicates rupture.
Can you visualise fetal head descent? – Absence of descent with a full‑term uterus raises suspicion of obstructed labour.

sections.p: Key points to remember for bedside and exam scenarios.
b: Palpate a firm, non‑tender lower uterine segment in late pregnancy
During caesarean, a transverse incision in the LUS reduces bleeding compared with a vertical incision

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain with fetal distress – suspect uterine rupture
Profuse vaginal bleeding after caesarean – suspect LUS haemorrhage
Inability to void after surgery – possible bladder injury

faq.q: Why is the lower uterine segment preferred for caesarean incision?
faq.a: It is thinner, less vascular, and heals with less scar, reducing future rupture risk.

faq.q: What sign suggests a bladder injury during caesarean?
faq.a: Clear fluid (urine) seen in the surgical field or postoperative gross haematuria.

faq.q: How can you assess LUS thickness without imaging?
faq.a: By palpating a smooth, thin area just above the bladder; a markedly thickened segment may indicate pathology.

exam: A 28‑year‑old in labour develops sudden severe lower abdominal pain and fetal bradycardia — what is your immediate diagnosis and management? — suspect uterine rupture at the LUS; call for emergency laparotomy, prepare blood, and give uterotonics after delivery.

During a caesarean you notice a clear fluid leaking from the incision site — what is the most likely injury and next step? — bladder injury; assess bladder integrity with methylene‑blue dye or saline, repair surgically, and insert catheter.

Explain why a transverse lower uterine segment incision reduces the risk of future uterine rupture compared with a classical vertical incision. — transverse incision follows muscle fibers, less tension, better healing; vertical incision cuts across fibers, higher scar weakness.

A patient in a district hospital presents with obstructed labour and a palpable firm lower uterine segment — what investigations are feasible and what do they tell you? — bedside ultrasound (if available) to assess fetal position; if not, clinical assessment of fetal descent and maternal vitals guide decision for operative delivery.

What are the main arterial sources to the lower uterine segment and why is this relevant in massive postpartum haemorrhage? — uterine and ovarian arteries; knowing them helps target uterine artery ligation or embolisation when bleeding persists.

During a caesarean you must decide where to place the incision in a uterus with a large fibroid occupying the upper segment — where do you incise and why? — lower uterine segment, because it avoids the fibroid, reduces bleeding and provides a safer plane.

A woman with a previous low transverse caesarean now presents in labour with a scar tenderness — what is the risk and how do you assess it? — risk of scar dehiscence; assess with ultrasound for scar thickness (<2 mm high risk) and monitor fetal heart tracing.

In a low‑resource setting, how would you manage a suspected LUS rupture when blood products are scarce? — rapid transfer to higher‑level centre, use of uterine tamponade (e.g., Foley catheter), and give tranexamic acid while arranging blood.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a systematic abdominal exam allow rapid identification of lower uterine segment (LUS) pathology in labour or after caesarean section.
b: Ask onset, character and radiation of pain; sudden tearing pain suggests rupture.
Ask about fetal heart rate changes, maternal vitals and any recent uterine manipulation.
Inquire about previous uterine scar type, number of caesareans and interval since last delivery.
Ask about bladder symptoms (dysuria, hematuria) that may indicate bladder injury.
Ask about obstetric history that predisposes to rupture (over‑distension, malpresentation, oxytocin use).

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, a limited panel of bedside and laboratory tests can confirm LUS rupture, quantify bleeding and guide resuscitation.
b: Full blood count – falling haemoglobin >2 g/dL within 1 hour suggests active hemorrhage.
Coagulation profile – PT/INR >1.5 or APTT >45 s signals consumptive coagulopathy; correct before surgery.
Serum lactate – >2 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion and need for aggressive resuscitation.
Portable ultrasound – presence of free fluid in Morrison’s pouch or pouch of Douglas confirms intra‑abdominal bleed; absence does not exclude rupture.
Uterine artery Doppler – low diastolic flow may indicate compromised perfusion but is not diagnostic of rupture.

sections.p: Classification of lower uterine segment injury follows the WHO/FIGO schema and guides operative planning and counselling.
b: LUS dehiscence – intact serosa with a visible myometrial gap; minimal bleeding, usually managed with repair only.
LUS rupture – full‑thickness tear with active bleeding and fetal extrusion; emergency laparotomy required.
Severity grade IV – associated bladder or ureteral injury, need multidisciplinary repair.

sections.p: A systematic approach saves lives when a lower uterine segment (LUS) rupture or massive haemorrhage is suspected in a low‑resource labour ward.
b: 1. Call for help, ensure two‑person team and gather sterile instruments.
2. Immediate resuscitation: give high‑flow oxygen, establish large‑bore IV lines, begin crystalloid bolus.
3. Rapid bedside ultrasound (FAST) to confirm intra‑uterine bleeding or free fluid in the peritoneum.
4. If the fetus is viable and delivery is imminent, proceed to emergency caesarean via a low transverse incision, avoiding extension into the uterine body.
5. Direct surgical control of bleeding: clamp and ligate uterine artery branches, apply uterine compression sutures (e.g., B‑Lynch) if bleeding persists.
6. If haemorrhage remains uncontrolled, consider internal iliac artery ligation or, as a last resort, hysterectomy.
7. Continuous monitoring: pulse, blood pressure, urine output, and estimated blood loss; transfuse packed red cells and plasma as soon as available.
8. Escalate to referral centre when blood products are exhausted, expertise for complex vascular control is lacking, or the patient is unstable despite maximal measures.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Pharmacologic adjuncts are essential for uterine atony and coagulopathy but must be used with awareness of adverse effects.
b: Oxytocin infusion – promotes uterine contraction; avoid rapid high‑dose bolus which can cause hypotension and tachycardia.
Carboprost tromethamine (15‑methyl‑PGF2α) – strong uterotonic; watch for bronchospasm, hypertension, and diarrhea; contraindicated in asthma.
Methylergometrine – useful when oxytocin fails; can cause severe hypertension and coronary spasm; avoid in pre‑eclampsia or hypertension.
Tranexamic acid – antifibrinolytic; reduces bleeding if given within 3 h of onset; monitor for seizures in renal failure.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) – prophylaxis for surgical site infection; adjust for local resistance patterns.
Avoid uterine tamponade packs for suspected rupture – they can worsen haemorrhage and delay definitive repair.

sections.p: Recognise early signs of failure to control bleeding or evolving organ dysfunction; act promptly.
b: Persistent hypotension (systolic < 90 mmHg) despite fluid and blood replacement – indicates ongoing haemorrhage; move to step 6 or refer.
Coagulopathy (PT/INR > 1.5, platelets < 50 × 10⁹/L) – start fresh frozen plasma and platelets; consider fibrinogen concentrate if available.
Uterine necrosis after aggressive compression sutures – monitor for foul discharge, fever, and rising white cell count; may need hysterectomy.
Bladder injury (gross haematuria, inability to fill bladder) – intra‑operative cystoscopy if possible; repair immediately.
Renal oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) – assess for hypovolemia or acute tubular injury; optimise perfusion and consider diuretics only after volume status is secure.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities common in low‑resource settings alter presentation, investigations and therapeutic choices for LUS emergencies.
b: HIV infection – may cause thrombocytopenia and anaemia; antiretroviral drugs can interact with carboprost (risk of hepatotoxicity).
Tuberculosis peritonitis – can mimic free fluid on ultrasound; look for chronic ascites, weight loss, and positive GeneXpert.
Severe malnutrition – reduces plasma protein, worsening bleeding; monitor albumin and give albumin if hypo‑albuminaemia is profound.
Pregnancy‑related anemia – baseline haemoglobin often < 11 g/dL; transfuse earlier to maintain oxygen delivery.
Diabetes mellitus – hyperglycaemia impairs wound healing; control glucose with insulin infusion, avoid high‑dose steroids.
Herbal remedies (e.g., neem, traditional uterotonics) – may contain unknown anticoagulants; ask specifically and document.
Chronic alcohol use – impairs coagulation and liver synthesis of clotting factors; correct with vitamin K and plasma.
Renal failure – limit oxytocin bolus, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, adjust tranexamic acid dose if needed.
Advanced maternal age (> 35 y) – higher risk of uterine atony and placenta previa; maintain a lower threshold for surgical control.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and treatment to the physiological differences and resource constraints of each population.
b: Children (adolescents) – uterine wall is thinner; use gentle uterotonics, avoid methylergometrine, and consider early referral for massive haemorrhage.
Pregnant women with prior low‑transverse scar – assess scar tenderness, use ultrasound to locate scar, and plan a repeat low‑transverse incision; avoid vertical incisions.
Elderly obstetric patients – higher incidence of uterine fibroids; pre‑operative MRI if available, otherwise ultrasound to map fibroid location before incision.
People living with HIV – ensure CD4 count and viral load are known; give prophylactic antibiotics covering opportunistic pathogens; monitor for drug‑drug interactions.

Low‑resource settings – rely on clinical assessment and bedside ultrasound; use uterine artery ligation and B‑Lynch sutures when blood products are scarce; have a clear referral pathway to a higher‑level centre.

facts: Lower uterine segment (LUS) extends from the internal cervical os to the peritoneal reflection on the anterior uterine wall, forming the inferior third of the uterus in the third trimester.
Transverse low‑segment caesarean incision is 2–3 cm above the bladder dome and 8–10 cm in length.
Uterine artery supplies 70 % of LUS blood; ovarian artery contributes the remaining 30 % via anastomoses at the lateral uterine border.
Pain from LUS incision is transmitted via T10–L1 dermatomes; loss of sensation above this level suggests nerve injury.
LUS thickness on ultrasound < 2 mm in late third trimester predicts higher risk of rupture during labour.
Bladder injury incidence during low‑segment caesarean is 0.5–1 %; intra‑operative cystoscopy detects 90 % of injuries.
Maternal mortality from uncontrolled LUS haemorrhage in low‑resource settings exceeds 5 % without timely blood transfusion.

vivas.q: Define the lower uterine segment and its anatomical limits.
vivas.a: The LUS is the thinned myometrial zone extending from the internal cervical os to the peritoneal reflection on the anterior uterine wall, constituting the inferior third of the uterus in late pregnancy.

vivas.q: Why is a transverse low‑segment incision preferred over a vertical incision for caesarean section?
vivas.a: It cuts across the less vascularised, thinner LUS, reduces intra‑operative blood loss, preserves uterine contractility, and lowers the risk of future uterine rupture.

vivas.q: What bedside sign indicates a possible LUS rupture during labour?
vivas.a: Sudden, severe lower abdominal pain with a firm, non‑tender LUS on palpation and fetal bradycardia; loss of uterine tone may be felt.

vivas.q: List the immediate surgical steps when LUS rupture is suspected.
vivas.a: 1. Call for help, 2. Rapid laparotomy, 3. Identify tear, 4. Apply uterine compression sutures, 5. Repair uterine edges with interrupted absorbable sutures, 6. Control bleeding (uterine artery ligation if needed), 7. Assess bladder integrity, 8. Resuscitate with fluids and blood.

vivas.q: How does portable Doppler assist in LUS emergencies?
vivas.a: It quickly assesses uterine artery flow; absent or markedly reduced flow suggests major vascular disruption, prompting urgent surgical control.

vivas.q: What ultrasound finding predicts LUS rupture risk?
vivas.a: LUS thickness < 2 mm measured in the sagittal plane during the third trimester.

vivas.q: Explain why uterine tamponade with gauze is contraindicated in LUS rupture.
vivas.a: Tamponade can increase pressure, worsen haemorrhage, and delay definitive repair; immediate surgical exploration is required.

vivas.q: Which arterial sources must be ligated first in massive LUS haemorrhage?
vivas.a: Uterine artery branches at the lateral uterine border; ovarian artery ligation is a secondary measure.

vivas.q: What are the key history questions when a woman in labour reports sudden lower abdominal pain?
vivas.a: Onset and character of pain, fetal movements, bleeding, previous caesarean scar, uterine surgery, and any recent trauma.

vivas.q: How to differentiate bladder injury from LUS rupture intra‑operatively?
vivas.a: Instill methylene blue into the bladder; leakage into the surgical field indicates bladder injury, whereas blood‑filled tear in the uterine wall indicates LUS rupture.

vivas.q: Which finding on a complete blood count is classically highlighted in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding?
vivas.a: A falling haemoglobin level with a raised mean corpuscular volume if chronic blood loss; acute bleed shows normal MCV initially.

vivas.q: Which part of the body experiences the initial acceleration during the somatic growth spurt in adolescents?
vivas.a: The distal femur and tibial growth plates accelerate first, followed by the spine.

vivas.q: Elongation of which part of the eye during adolescent growth may result in myopia?
vivas.a: Axial length of the globe increases, leading to myopia.

vivas.q: Which fungal pathogen is part of the established spectrum of opportunistic infections in HIV/AIDS?
vivas.a: Cryptococcus neoformans.

vivas.q: Which clinical finding forms part of the insulin resistance syndrome often accompanying pre‑diabetes and childhood type 2 diabetes?
vivas.a: Acanthosis nigricans on the neck or axillae.

vivas.q: Which factor has contributed to the global resurgence of malaria in many parts of the tropics?
vivas.a: Insecticide resistance in Anopheles vectors.

vivas.q: Which clinical finding is part of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria?
vivas.a: Temperature > 38 °C or < 36 °C.

vivas.q: A patient with atopic dermatitis presents with a new rash. Which condition is part of the 'atopic triad' that often coexists with atopic dermatitis?
vivas.a: Allergic rhinitis.

vivas.q: List and explain the hand‑hygiene steps required as part of aseptic technique.
vivas.a: 1. Wet hands, 2. Apply soap, 3. Scrub all surfaces for 20 seconds, 4. Rinse, 5. Dry with disposable towel, 6. Use towel to turn off tap.

vivas.q: Outline the primary functions of bile in the human body.
vivas.a: Emulsifies dietary fats, facilitates absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins, and excretes bilirubin and cholesterol.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman in labour suddenly develops severe lower abdominal pain, fetal bradycardia and a firm lower uterine segment on palpation. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
mcqs.e: Sudden pain with a firm LUS suggests rupture; rapid surgical exploration is required.

mcqs.q: During a caesarean section the surgeon notes clear fluid leaking from the incision before the uterus is opened. Which structure is most likely injured?
mcqs.e: Clear fluid is urine; bladder dome lies directly anterior to the LUS.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a recommended step in managing a suspected LUS rupture in a low‑resource setting?
o: Uterine artery ligation if bleeding persists
mcqs.e: Tamponade is contraindicated and may worsen bleeding.

mcqs.q: Which ultrasound measurement best predicts LUS rupture risk in the third trimester?
mcqs.e: A thinned LUS (< 2 mm) correlates with higher rupture risk.

mcqs.q: A 25‑year‑old woman with obstructed labour has a palpable firm lower uterine segment. Which bedside maneuver helps confirm LUS rupture?
mcqs.e: Bimanual exam can feel a rent in the LUS, confirming rupture.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a common complication of a low‑segment caesarean incision in low‑resource hospitals?
mcqs.e: The bladder lies directly anterior to the LUS, making it vulnerable during incision.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old primigravida at 39 weeks presents with sudden, severe lower abdominal pain, a firm lower uterine segment on palpation, and fetal heart rate 80 bpm.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Uterine rupture involving the lower uterine segment.

qs.q: What immediate management steps should be taken?
qs.a: Call for help, start IV fluids, prepare for emergency laparotomy, deliver the fetus, repair the uterine tear, control bleeding, assess bladder integrity.

qs.q: Which intra‑operative finding would confirm bladder injury?
qs.a: Leakage of clear fluid (urine) from the bladder dome, especially after instilling methylene blue.

mistakes: Applying a gauze tamponade for suspected LUS rupture instead of immediate surgical repair.
Skipping uterine artery ligation during massive haemorrhage and attempting ovarian artery ligation first.
Assuming a thin LUS (< 2 mm) guarantees rupture; it is a risk factor but not diagnostic alone.
Omitting sequential numbering of management steps, leading to missed actions during emergencies.
Confusing the anatomical extent of the LUS, describing it as the upper uterine body rather than the inferior third.
